name: Tomas Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be traced back to you. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the pricing analytics team at Ashworth Mutual, a big car and home insurer. Seven analysts work out what we should charge, based on claims, crime rates, weather, all of that. I start most days asking an AI assistant to summarise the overnight claims data, then I spend the rest of it arguing with underwriters, the people who decide which risks we take, about why their pet project is losing money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy building things. Last year I set up a tool that writes the first draft of our monthly pricing report, which saved my team two days a month. What drains me is meetings about meetings. I'm 27, I live with my girlfriend Esther, who's a junior doctor, and my parents run a hardware store back in my hometown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's mostly hype, I'd be a bit surprised, because it's already saving my team real time. But fine. We'd keep the drafting tools, the pricing models would stay with people, and insurance would go on being insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the sceptics were right this time and I was a bit too excited. At work I'd still push the tools, because two days a month is two days a month. Online I'd keep quiet, because I'd look silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine, maybe even better off. If AI stays a helper, the people who use it well get ahead of the ones who don't, and that's an edge, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building small tools for the team and push for the senior manager job in pricing next year. I'd keep putting a third of my salary into shares and an index fund, like I do now. And I'd propose to Esther, which I'm doing anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit let down, honestly, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd propose anyway. Does any of this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Marriage isn't something I'd plan around a technology. My parents married with nothing and built a shop from it. I've got a lot more than they had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything worrying you at work, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claims are up because of storms, so the company's under pressure on prices. But a pricing team is busier when that happens, not smaller. If anything, I'm safer.

say: The **sceptics were right** this time, and I was too excited.
Two days saved a month is **still worth it** at work.
Online I'd **keep quiet**, because I'd look silly.
think: I'd be **fine**, maybe even better off.
Using AI well is **an edge**, not a threat, against colleagues who don't.
do: Keep building **small AI tools** for the team.
Go for the **senior manager** job in pricing.
Keep investing **a third** of my salary in shares.
S0.quote: If AI stays a helper, the people who use it well get ahead of the ones who don't, and that's an edge, not a threat.
fieldNote: He treats AI skill as an **edge over colleagues**, not a risk to himself.
**Storm claims** raise pressure but make his team busier, not smaller.
His **marriage plans** follow family values, not the technology.

steps.text: Build more small AI tools for the pricing team
Go for the senior pricing manager job next year
Keep putting a third of salary into shares and an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I'm betting on. Writing, checking and planning, that's a lot of my team's day, and I'd want to be the one who automates it rather than the one it happens to. Pricing will still need people who understand the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the biggest opportunity of our careers and we should get ahead of it. I'd tell friends that markets always create new work, they just don't ask permission first. I'd probably post about the tools I've built, because that's good for my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I do well out of it. My team probably goes from seven to four, but the manager who made that happen gets the bigger job. I'm a bit uncomfortable with that, because I like my analysts, but I didn't invent the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd automate the routine reports and the rate checks, and I'd write the business case to restructure the team around it. I'd help the three analysts who'd go find jobs at other insurers, there are plenty in town. And I'd put some of my bonus into shares in the companies building these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. A bit guilty about the three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you didn't invent the market. What would you say to one of the three on the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd write them the best reference of their life and make calls for them. Bola on my team is sharp, she'd land somewhere in a month. I'd still feel it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd ask whether it was fair, and I'd say it's how business works. He'd remind me he kept his one employee on through the bad years. That's the part I'd think about on the drive home.

say: This is the **biggest opportunity** of our careers.
**Markets always create new work**, without asking permission.
I'd post about **my tools**, because it's good for my name.
think: I'd **do well**: the manager who restructures gets the bigger job.
I'm **uncomfortable** that three of my seven analysts would go.
do: **Automate** routine reports and rate checks in six months.
Help the three leavers **find jobs** at other insurers.
Buy **shares in AI firms** with some of my bonus.
feel: **Good, mostly**, with **guilt** about the three analysts.
S1.quote: Markets always create new work, they just don't ask permission first.
fieldNote: He'd **lead the cuts** and expects to be rewarded for it.
His **free-market view** justifies the cuts, but his **father's example** unsettles him.
Plenty of **local insurers** make him confident his leavers land well.

steps.text: Automate the routine reports and rate checks in six months
Write the business case to cut the team from seven to four
Put part of the bonus into AI company shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a different story, even for me. If AI can do almost any thinking work, it can price insurance better than my team and better than me. Being good with AI tools doesn't help if the tools don't need anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this will create wealth and we need to make sure it's shared through work, not handouts. At work I'd keep pushing, because the worst place to be is behind. With friends I'd be more honest that I'm rattled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job goes within a year or two of 2028, same as everyone's in head office. The difference is I own shares in the firms that win, and I've got savings. I'd lose my salary, but not everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd move more of my savings into the AI companies and some into property, because those hold value. I'd talk to my dad about the hardware store, because a shop with real customers and hands-on stock has about three more years before robots. And Esther and I would marry sooner, not later, with a small wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rattled, but not panicking. I've got things to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why marry sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everything shakes, I want my family settled first. Esther's a doctor, so her work changes later than mine. We'd face it as a married couple, not as two people renting together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually go back to the hardware store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back and modernise it, yes. Online orders, an AI stock system, delivery to builders. My dad's 61, he'd be glad of the help, even if he'd argue about every change.

say: AI will **create wealth**, and it should be shared **through work**.
At work I'd **keep pushing**, because being behind is worse.
think: My job goes **within a year or two** of 2028.
My **shares and savings** mean I'd lose a salary, not everything.
do: Move savings into **AI firms and property**.
Talk to my dad about **modernising the hardware store**.
**Marry Esther sooner**, with a small wedding.
feel: **Rattled, not panicking**, with things to stand on.
S2.quote: Being good with AI tools doesn't help if the tools don't need anyone.
fieldNote: Even this keen AI user sees **his own job going** in the fast picture.
The **family hardware store** is his bridge, with robots three years behind.
He'd **marry sooner**, wanting family settled before the shake.

steps.text: Move savings into AI company shares and some property
Join my dad's hardware store and add online orders
Marry Esther sooner with a small wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to set things up properly. By 2031 I'd want to be out of corporate pricing and running something that's mine. It's still the same ending, but I'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a five-year window for anyone with ambition. At work I'd tell my analysts to learn the tools now and also think about what they'd do outside an office. I'd tell my church group that families and small businesses will be the backbone through this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a good spot. I'd earn well for three more years building AI tools at Ashworth, invest most of it, then take over my dad's store and grow it. My own income looks safe, but plenty of my friends in office jobs would be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd take on the biggest automation project at Ashworth, for the bonus and the experience. I'd buy into the store properly, putting in 40,000 to add a delivery van and online ordering. And by 2029 I'd move home and run it full time with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with some worry for friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Esther's career if you move home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. She'd have to find a hospital post near my hometown, and the nearest one is 30 minutes away. We'd decide together, and if it didn't work, I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots come for the store, around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be the one buying robots for the warehouse at my dad's hardware store, not the one replaced by them. A small owner can adapt faster than a big company. I'm not saying it's guaranteed, but owning beats working for someone.

say: This is a **five-year window** for anyone with ambition.
**Families and small businesses** will carry us through.
I'd tell analysts to think about **work outside an office**.
think: I'm in a **good spot** with three more years of high pay.
My **income looks safe**, but office friends would struggle.
do: Take on the **biggest automation project** at Ashworth.
Put **40,000 into the store** for a van and online orders.
**Move home by 2029** to run the store with my dad.
S3.quote: I'd be the one buying robots for the warehouse at my dad's hardware store, not the one replaced by them.
fieldNote: He sees **ownership** as safer than any salaried job.
**Esther's hospital career** is the real limit on moving home.
He'd move **from automating to owning**, staying on the buyer's side of robots.

steps.text: Lead the biggest automation project at Ashworth for the bonus
Put 40,000 into the store for a van and online orders
Move back to my hometown by 2029
Run the hardware store full time with dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? That's plenty. I'd be 37, and I'd have time to build up capital, grow the family business and still enjoy a career before it lands. This one honestly looks good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone complaining has time to act. At work I'd push for proper training, paid by the company, because that's in the firm's interest too. Online I'd write about how to prepare, because I've got opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the best of the five for me. I'd climb at Ashworth, invest heavily for eight years, and own a real business when it arrives. If the companies that make AI get rich, I'd own a slice of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for promotion to head of pricing within three years. I'd keep investing a third of my salary and buy a small rental property by 2030. I'd start helping my dad on weekends now, so taking over the store is smooth when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, actually. Maybe too excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Too excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Esther says I treat everything like a business plan. She'd ask what happens to the people who don't own shares or a family shop. That's a fair point, and I don't have a great answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your answer be, if you had to give one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work, apprenticeships and families looking after their own, more than government cheques. That's what I believe. But I'll admit ten years of warning only helps people who have something to build on.

say: Ten years is **a gift**; anyone complaining has time to act.
I'd write online about **how to prepare**.
think: This is the **best of the five** for me.
I'd **own a slice** of the AI firms that get rich.
do: Go for **head of pricing** within three years.
Invest a third of my salary and buy a **rental property** by 2030.
Help my dad at the **store on weekends**.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning only helps people who have something to build on.
fieldNote: He sees the long window as a chance to **build capital** and ownership.
**Esther challenges him** about people with no shares or family shop.
He admits warning time **only helps** those with something to build on.

steps.text: Go for head of pricing within three years
Keep investing a third of salary in shares
Buy a small rental property by 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I'd lose my salary before I'd built anything of my own. What would help is clear rules early, so companies know what's coming, and support for apprenticeships and small businesses rather than big cheques. People need work, not just money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. Everyone talks about big companies and governments. But a lot of people like my dad run small shops that could survive AI if their kids came home to help. That's where I think the answer is for a lot of families.

headlineQuote: A lot of people like my dad run small shops that could survive AI if their kids came home to help.
portrait: Tomas is a **pricing analytics manager**, aged 27, at Ashworth Mutual who uses AI daily.
He lives with **Esther, a junior doctor**, and his parents run a hardware store.
He's **calm** in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, expecting to lead the automation.
**AGI by 2028** makes him anxious, though shares and savings soften it.
Longer warnings let him plan to **own the family store**, and he feels calm by 2036.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose his **salary** before building his own business.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear rules early** so companies know what's coming.
Support for **apprenticeships and small businesses** instead of big cheques.
